n: Boaz goes straight to the city gate, the town's public square and courtroom. The nearer relative happens by, and Boaz calls him over. The narrator leaves him unnamed — he never earns a lasting name.

f.g: The gate area was where business, legal cases, and public agreements were settled before witnesses.
Hebrew peloni almoni, roughly “so-and-so” — the narrator withholds his name.

n: Boaz gathers ten elders as official witnesses, making this a legally binding public proceeding.
Boaz raises the matter: Naomi must sell (or transfer the rights to) the land that belonged to Elimelech, and a relative has the right to keep it in the family.
Boaz formally offers the nearer kinsman first right to redeem the land, with himself next in line. Gaining extra land seems attractive, so the man agrees.

f.g: To buy back property or people so they stay within the family; the same idea is used for the Lord's redeeming of His people.

n: Then Boaz reveals the catch: whoever takes the land also takes responsibility for Ruth, marrying her so that a son can carry on the dead husband's name and inherit the land.

f.w: raise up the name of the dead

n: The relative backs out. A son born to Ruth would inherit the land, so his investment would not benefit his own estate. He gives his right to Boaz.

f.g: damage or endanger my own estate

n: The narrator explains an old custom: to seal a transfer of rights, a man removed his sandal and gave it to the other party, like signing a contract.

f.g: A sandal may have symbolized the right to walk on and possess land.

n: The relative tells Boaz to buy it himself and hands over his sandal, completing the legal transfer.
Boaz publicly declares that he has acquired all the property of Elimelech and his sons from Naomi, and calls the crowd to witness.
Boaz also declares that he takes Ruth as his wife to preserve Mahlon's name and inheritance. His willingness to give, rather than gain, shows true redemption.

f.g: acquired; here a legal term for taking on the marriage responsibility, not buying a slave.
not forgotten or erased from the family records

n: The witnesses bless the marriage, praying Ruth will be like Rachel and Leah, the mothers of Israel's tribes, and that Boaz will prosper and be honored.
They also wish Boaz's family to be like that of Pharez, Judah's son by Tamar — another story in which an outsider woman preserved a family line, and Boaz's own ancestor.

f.w: Pharez, whom Tamar bare unto Judah

n: Boaz marries Ruth, and the Lord grants her a son. The text credits God with the gift of conception, the quiet hand of God showing again.
The women of Bethlehem praise the Lord for giving Naomi a redeemer. The empty woman of chapter 1 is now full.

f.g: Here the go'el is the baby boy, who will carry on the family name.

n: This grandson will renew Naomi's life and care for her in old age. And the women honor Ruth: her love is worth more than seven sons — the ideal number of a perfect family.

f.g: Literally, “one who brings back your soul” — the same verb as Naomi's “returning” in chapter 1.

n: Naomi holds the baby close and helps raise him. The woman who lost everything now cradles new life.

f.g: Here, a caregiver or guardian, not a wet nurse.

n: The neighbors name the child Obed, and the narrator reveals the surprise: he is grandfather of King David. A Moabite convert's faithfulness leads to Israel's royal line.
A closing genealogy traces the family from Pharez, son of Judah, forward. Genealogies in scripture show how God's promises unfold across generations.
The line continues through Hezron and Ram to Amminadab, whose daughter married Aaron.
Nahshon was leader of the tribe of Judah during the wilderness journey with Moses. Salmon is listed in Matthew as married to Rahab of Jericho.
Salmon is the father of Boaz, and Boaz the father of Obed. If Matthew's record is followed, both Boaz's mother (Rahab) and his wife (Ruth) were converts from outside Israel.
The book ends with David, Israel's great king. Through David's line would come Jesus Christ, the ultimate Redeemer, born in this same town of Bethlehem.
